sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Find the probability their sum is $8$.
questions.answer: Total outcomes: $n(S)=36$. Favorable outcomes (sum $=8$): $(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2)$ — that's $5$.

questions.q: How many ways can a committee of $4$ be chosen from $10$ people?
questions.answer: Order doesn't matter, so use combinations: $\binom{10}{4}=\frac{10!}{4!\,6!}=\frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7}{4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}=210$.
questions.explanation: Order doesn't matter, so use combinations: $\binom{10}{4}=\frac{10!}{4!\,6!}=\frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7}{4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}=210$.

questions.q: How many ways can $2$ officers (president, vice president — order matters) be chosen from $6$ candidates?
questions.answer: Order matters, so use permutations: $P(6,2)=\frac{6!}{4!}=6\cdot5=30$.

questions.q: Explain, using Theorem 6.1, how $\binom{6}{2}$ relates to $P(6,2)$ from the previous question.
questions.answer: Theorem 6.1 says $\binom{6}{2}=\frac{P(6,2)}{2!}=\frac{30}{2}=15$ — combinations undercount permutations by exactly the $2!$ orderings of each chosen pair.
questions.explanation: Theorem 6.1 says $\binom{6}{2}=\frac{P(6,2)}{2!}=\frac{30}{2}=15$ — combinations undercount permutations by exactly the $2!$ orderings of each chosen pair.

questions.q: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A)=0.4$ and $P(B)=0.5$. Find $P(A\ \mathrm{and}\ B)$.
questions.target: Independent events and the addition rule
questions.answer: By Definition 6.4, $P(A\ \mathrm{and}\ B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)=(0.4)(0.5)=0.2$.

questions.q: A card is drawn from a standard $52$-card deck. Find $P(\mathrm{Queen}\ \mathrm{or}\ \mathrm{Spade})$.
questions.target: Independent events and the addition rule
questions.answer: $P(\mathrm{Queen})=\frac{4}{52}$, $P(\mathrm{Spade})=\frac{13}{52}$, and $P(\mathrm{Queen}\ \mathrm{and}\ \mathrm{Spade})=\frac{1}{52}$ (the Queen of Spades).

questions.q: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A)=0.6$ and $P(B)=0.3$. Find $P(A\ \mathrm{and}\ B)$.
questions.answer: By the independence rule, $P(A\ \mathrm{and}\ B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)=(0.6)(0.3)=\frac{9}{50}$.

questions.q: Out of $27$ equally likely boxes, $7$ are labeled, $8$ are sealed, and $7$ are both. One item is chosen at random. Find $P(\mathrm{labeled}\ \mathrm{or}\ \mathrm{sealed})$.
questions.answer: By the addition rule: $P(\mathrm{labeled}\ \mathrm{or}\ \mathrm{sealed})=\frac{7}{27}+\frac{8}{27}-\frac{7}{27}=\frac{8}{27}$.

questions.q: Out of $37$ equally likely numbers, $4$ are even, $10$ are prime, and $2$ are both. One item is chosen at random. Find $P(\mathrm{even}\ \mathrm{or}\ \mathrm{prime})$.
questions.target: Independent events and the addition rule
questions.answer: By the addition rule: $P(\mathrm{even}\ \mathrm{or}\ \mathrm{prime})=\frac{4}{37}+\frac{10}{37}-\frac{2}{37}=\frac{12}{37}$.

A continuous random variable $X$ is uniformly distributed over the interval $[2, 10]$. What is $P(4 \leq X \leq 7)$?
questions.answer: Probability density $f(x) = \frac{1}{10 - 2} = \frac{1}{8}$. $P(4 \leq X \leq 7) = \frac{7 - 4}{8} = \frac{3}{8}$.

questions.q: In any continuous probability distribution, what is $P(X = c)$ for any single exact point $c$?
questions.answer: For any continuous distribution, the probability of taking any single exact real value is $0$ because the area of a single line is zero.

questions.q: Given $P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.3,$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$, are events $A$ and $B$ independent?
choices: Yes, because they are mutually exclusive
questions.answer: $P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B) = 0.6 + 0.3 - 0.7 = 0.20$. For independence, $P(A)P(B) = 0.6 \times 0.3 = 0.18$. Since $0.20 \neq 0.18$, they are not independent.
questions.explanation: $P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B) = 0.6 + 0.3 - 0.7 = 0.20$. For independence, $P(A)P(B) = 0.6 \times 0.3 = 0.18$. Since $0.20 \neq 0.18$, they are not independent.

questions.q: A point is chosen at random inside a square of side $10$. What is the probability that it falls inside the inscribed circle?
questions.answer: Area of square $= 10^2 = 100$. Inscribed circle radius $= 5$, Area $= \pi(5^2) = 25\pi$. Probability $= \frac{25\pi}{100} = \frac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.785$.
questions.explanation: Area of square $= 10^2 = 100$. Inscribed circle radius $= 5$, Area $= \pi(5^2) = 25\pi$. Probability $= \frac{25\pi}{100} = \frac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.785$.
